Case 1: Impacted second molars
How expert input is used
This script combines the Case 1 records with the expert panel interviews. Experts 1 and 2 are orthodontists and carry the most weight. Expert 3 is an oral surgeon: his views are weighted lower on orthodontic planning, but carry full weight on surgery, exposure and tooth removal decisions. Each phase ends with an "Expert basis" line so faculty can trace every point.
Information shown to the student
A 13-year-old Chinese female. Her chief complaint is protruding upper front teeth and a lower tooth "growing inside."
No relevant medical history, no known drug allergies.
Growth status: 1.5 years post-menarche.
OJ 5 mm, OB 50%.
Upper dental midline 1 mm right of the facial midline; lower dental midline 2 mm right.
No functional shift.
Case summary for the tutor (not shown to the student)
This 13-year-old Chinese female has no relevant medical or dental history and no known drug allergies. Caries and periodontal disease are controlled.
Skeletal. Class II div 1 malocclusion on an average-angle Class I skeletal base.
Occlusion. Incisors Class II div 1, increased OJ 5 mm, increased OB 50%. Canines right ¼ unit Class III, left ¼ unit Class II. Molars right ½ unit Class III, left ¼ unit Class III. Crossbite #12/#83. Scissors bite at #14 and #27. No CR–MI slide (aka functional shift). Upper midline deviated 1 mm right, lower midline deviated 2 mm right of the facial midline.
Teeth. Upper #17–#27 present; #17 partially erupted and #27 erupted, both erupting buccally. Lower #37–#47 present. Retained #83 with #43 erupted lingually (the patient's "lower tooth growing inside"). #37 partially erupted and mesially impacted. #47 more erupted than #37, with more crown visible, and also mesially impacted. All four third molars present and unerupted.
Arches. Both ovoid. Mild upper crowding with proclined upper incisors. Moderate lower crowding.
OPG. #37 mesially angulated about 40–60° to #36, mesial marginal ridge locked under the distal bulge of #36 at CEJ level, roots two-thirds to almost complete with open apices; #38 developing (crown formed, roots starting) distal to the #37 roots, normal eruption direction. #47 mesially angulated about 30–40° to #46, locked in the same way at CEJ level, roots two-thirds to almost complete with open apices, and sitting more superiorly than #37; #48 developing like #38. #17 partially erupted, not impacted. #27 erupted. #18 and #28 present and developing.
Anterior maxillary occlusal. No abnormal findings (no supernumerary or midline pathology).
Bitewings. #37 and #47 mesially impacted against the first molars. No caries seen on the distal surface of second molars.
Lateral ceph. SNA, SNB, ANB, FMA, MMA, LAFH, lower incisor inclination, L1–APog and lower lip to E-line within normal limits: Class I skeletal base, normodivergent, normal LAFH. Wits increased, upper incisor inclination increased, interincisal angle decreased.
Expert panel view of Case 1 (tutor background)
Prognosis: good for both second molars; #47 slightly better because it sits higher and shows more crown for bonding. All three experts agreed.
Keep both second molars. No expert recommended extracting a second molar. At 13 the third molars' final morphology is unpredictable, so they are not a reliable replacement.
Space: the orthodontists favoured premolar extractions, so the first molars can be mesialised and the second molars uprighted. Expert 2 suggested upper first premolars, #44 and #35.
Third molars: remove them if the second molars must be distalised and the third molars are in the way (Expert 1). The oral surgeon preferred removing the third molars over the second molars because of unpredictable third molar morphology.
Mechanics: bond a tube where possible; piggyback with open coil or an uprighting spring or lever arm; favour root mesialisation over crown distalisation where the third molars are close.
Where the experts differed: the oral surgeon thought the case could be managed non-extraction with third molar removal and distalisation. The orthodontists preferred extractions given the crowding and overjet.
Part 1: The six phases
Phase 1: Observe the records
What the student sees
Goal: Describe what you see in the history, clinical findings and records, then say what you think the main problems are and how sure you can be from these records alone.
Opening question: Looking through the records, what is the patient's chief complaint, and what do you notice about her malocclusion?
Records available in this phase: history, clinical findings, intraoral photos, study models, OPG, anterior maxillary occlusal radiograph, bitewings radiograph, lateral ceph reading and tracing.
Clinical finding available in this phase: #37 is partially erupted. #47 is more erupted than #37, with more crown showing in the mouth.
What the tutor looks for, and what it reveals if a student is stuck
No.
What the tutor looks for
What the tutor reveals
1.1
Records the chief complaint, age and growth status.
She's 13 and 1.5 years past menarche. Her complaint is about her front teeth, so the impacted molars will most likely be treated as part of comprehensive orthodontic treatment.
1.2
Links the "lower tooth growing inside" to the retained #83 with #43 erupted lingually.
The lower right primary canine #83, is still there, so #43 has erupted lingually. That's the tooth she's noticed.
1.3
Identifies #37 and #47 as mesially impacted rather than simply late, relating her age to the normal eruption time of second molars.
At 13, second molars are usually erupted. Both lower second molars are mesially angulated and their mesial marginal ridges are locked under the distal bulge of the first molars at CEJ level. So this is impaction, not just late eruption.
1.4
Checks the impaction sites for food trapping, caries and how well she can keep them clean, and uses this to judge urgency.
A partially erupted, impacted molar traps food. However, there is no caries seen on the first molar and seems to be able to keep the area clean, so nothing is forcing urgent treatment.
1.5
Names at least two relevant occlusal findings: Class II div 1 incisors, increased OJ/OB, crossbite #12/#83, scissors bite #14 and #27, crowding, non-coincident midlines, or the canine and molar relationships.
Her incisors are Class II div 1 with increased OJ at 5mm and increased OB at 50%. There is crossbite at #12/#83, scissors bites at #14 and #27, upper mild crowding, moderate lower crowding, and both upper and lower dental midlines deviated to the right.
1.6
Notes how much of each second molar crown is exposed, and that this decides whether an attachment can be bonded.
#47 shows more crown in the mouth than #37. That matters because you need enough tooth surface to bond a tube before you can upright it, which also points to ease, speed and prognosis of uprighting it.
 
Bonus points
Review the whole OPG before the teeth: condyles, bone, sinuses, any pathology.
Compares the two sides and notes that #47 looks more favourable than #37.
Considers the opposing occlusion and interocclusal clearance, noting the upper second molars are erupting buccally and #27 is in scissors bite.
Notes all four third molars are present, without making them a requirement in this phase.
Follow-up questions (the tutor may use these word for word)
What does she mean by a tooth "growing inside"?
At 13, which teeth would you expect to be fully erupted well into the arch that aren't?
Which second molar shows more crown in the mouth, and why does that matter?
Is there anything about the impaction area that would make you treat it sooner?
How would you describe her bite? Note some occlusal findings.
Instructions to the tutor (not shown to students)
Keep the recorded context separate from interpretation: she is 13, 1.5 years post-menarche, with no relevant medical history, and caries and periodontally controlled.
Before discussing prognosis or treatment, the student should record the retained #83 with lingual #43, both impacted second molars, and at least two occlusal findings.
The case does not record her stated wish for comprehensive treatment, or the interocclusal clearance. If the student asks, accept it as a sensible question; say her complaint about her front teeth suggests she is open to full treatment, and do not invent a measurement.
The OPG is enough to describe angulation and locking; the bitewings add a clearer view of the contacts.
No 3D imaging is available for this case. Never suggest or ask about it. If a student asks for it, say it isn't available and ask what the 2D records show.
Expert basis: Experts 1 and 2 (orthodontists): patient's wish for comprehensive treatment, age relative to eruption timing, food trap / caries / hygiene setting urgency, crown exposure for bonding, #47 more crown visible. Expert 1: opposing occlusion and interocclusal clearance. Expert 3 (oral surgeon): holistic OPG review (bonus only).

Phase 2: Characterise the impaction
What the student sees
Goal: Use the records to describe exactly how each second molar is impacted, and what each record can and can't show you.
Opening question: How would you describe the impaction of #37 and #47, and what does each record tell you about it and its surroundings?
Record available from this phase: same as phase 1.
What the tutor looks for, and what it reveals if a student is stuck
No.
What the tutor looks for
What the tutor reveals
2.1
Describes the angulation of each molar, classifies it as mesioangular (not horizontal or vertical), and identifies #37 as the more tipped.
Both #37 and #47 are impacted with mesial inclination, although #37 has more severe angulation thus impaction. Mesioangular is a more favourable pattern than horizontal.
2.2
Describes the vertical depth: the mesial marginal ridge locked under the distal bulge of the first molar at CEJ level.
On both sides the mesial marginal ridges are locked under the distal bulge of the first molars at CEJ level. #47 sits slightly higher than #37, which is another reason it may be easier to manage.
2.3
Records root development (about two-thirds to almost complete, apices open) and considers root shape and root position.
Both roots are two-thirds to almost formed with open ends. There is higher risk to mobility and root resorption for root shape that is short or conical, and root position that is located far distally.
2.4
Records third molar position and whether the third molars would get in the way if the second molars were moved back.
The lower third molars are present with crowns formed and their roots just starting. It is located behind the second molar roots. If you push the second molar crowns back, they could collide with the third molar teeth.
2.5
Considers the space behind each second molar, including how close it is to the ascending ramus.
Look at the space available behind each second molar crown and how near it is to the ramus. There’s some room to move the crowns distally, but the third molars are developing in that area.
 
Bonus points
Distinguishes impaction (a physical obstruction, here the first molar's distal bulge) from primary failure of eruption (no obstruction), and links the cause to prognosis.
Notes the molars are caught mainly against the adjacent tooth rather than buried in bone, which is more favourable.
Checks for a visible periodontal ligament space around the second molars.
Notes the OPG can distort angulation, so the bitewing gives a more reliable view of the contact.
Follow-up questions (the tutor may use these word for word)
What do the x-rays show the second molar crowns are caught against?
Is this impaction mesioangular, horizontal or vertical? Why does that matter?
Which molar sits deeper, and how does that affect treatment?
What do the roots of #37 and #47 tell you about their development?
How do the root shape and position affect the risks?
Is there space available behind each second molar?
If you moved the second molars back, what might they run into?
Instructions to the tutor (not shown to students)
Treat the bitewing and OPG findings in the case summary as the source-backed description. Never claim the model read image pixels.
Keep angulation, vertical depth, root development and shape, third molar position and posterior space as separate descriptors.
Accept mesioangular. Do not accept horizontal or vertical.
Root resorption risk cannot be predicted definitively from these records. If asked, the expected answer is to assume it may happen and consent the patient for it.
The case summary does not report caries or resorption on the distal surfaces of #36 and #46. Do not invent findings there. If the student raises it, accept it as a sensible thing to check.
No 3D imaging is available for this case. Do not suggest it. If asked, say it isn't available and redirect to the 2D records.
Expert basis: Experts 1 and 2: angulation (mesioangular more favourable than horizontal or vertical), vertical depth, caries, third molar collision on distalisation, posterior space and ramus, distal root position needing more time, conical roots and resorption risk "assume and consent". Expert 1: #47 more superiorly positioned; aetiology (impaction vs PFE). Expert 2: visible PDL. Expert 3: tooth impaction rather than bony impaction (bonus only).

Phase 3: Assess the prognosis
What the student sees
Goal: Weigh what makes it more or less likely that each second molar can be uprighted into the arch, and what could go wrong.
Opening question: How likely is it that #37 and #47 can be uprighted into the arch, and what makes each more or less likely?
What the tutor looks for, and what it reveals if a student is stuck
No.
What the tutor looks for
What the tutor reveals
3.1
Assesses prognosis for each molar from several factors together: angulation, depth, crown exposure for bonding, root development, space and third molar position.
Both molars have a good prognosis: they're mesioangular, can be seen in the arch, bondable, caries-free, and the roots are still open. #47 is slightly better because it is more erupted and shows more crown.
3.2
Recognises that her age and open apices favour treatment now: the tooth moves more readily and bone and gum heal better in a young patient.
At a young age with open root ends, the molars move more easily, and the bone and gum recover better after uprighting.
3.3
Links prognosis to space: creating space in front (extractions with first molar mesialisation) makes uprighting easier than relying on distalisation alone.
Uprighting is much easier if the first molars can move forward into extraction space. If you can only push the second molars back, the third molars and ramus may limit us.
3.4
Recognises that keeping the second molars is preferable to replacing them with the third molars, because third molar size and shape are still unpredictable at age 13.
Second molars are valuable functional units. At 13 the wisdom teeth have barely started forming their roots, so we can't yet tell if they'd make a good replacement. That favours saving the second molars especially if their prognosis is not poor.
3.5
Names the main risks of uprighting: root resorption, mobility, a periodontal pocket or bony defect distal to the second molar, and an open contact with food trapping.
Risks include root shortening, mobility, deep pocket or bone defect behind the molar, and a gap that traps food. These are less likely in a young patient but should be discussed with her.
 
Bonus points
Notes that waiting is unlikely to help: molars locked at CEJ level are unlikely to right themselves.
Notes that her growth stage affects the skeletal side of the plan but does not drive second molar eruption.
Plans a progress checkpoint, with escalation if a molar does not respond.
Follow-up questions (the tutor may use these word for word)
What about each molar makes it easier or harder to upright?
Why might #47 be easier than #37?
How would your view change if she were 30 years old?
Where could the space for uprighting come from?
Would you rather keep the second molars or the wisdom teeth? Why?
What would you warn her about before starting?
Instructions to the tutor (not shown to students)
The expert view is that both molars have a good prognosis, with #47 slightly better. Do not describe #37 as poor or guarded.
Assess prognosis from several factors together. Do not reduce it to one factor.
Do not require a specific uprighting technique in this phase. That belongs to Phase 5.
Root resorption risk cannot be measured from the records; accept "assume it may happen and consent the patient".
Expert basis: All three experts: prognosis good for both molars, #47 slightly better. Experts 1 and 2: space via lower extractions and first molar mesialisation improves prognosis; keep two molars where possible; risks of resorption, mobility, distal pocket, open contact. Expert 2: perio defects less likely in young patients. Expert 3 (weighted, removal decision): third molar morphology unpredictable at 13, so keep the second molars; younger bone and healing more favourable.

Phase 5: Compare management options
What the student sees
Goal: Put forward a treatment plan for both arches that includes the impacted second molars, justify it, and weigh it against the alternatives.
Opening question: What treatment plan would you propose for this patient, including the impacted second molars, and why?
What the tutor looks for, and what it reveals if a student is stuck
No.
What the tutor looks for
What the tutor reveals
5.1
Gives one justified plan addressing both arches: overjet, crowding, lingual #43, crossbite, scissors bites and midlines. An extraction plan is expected given the moderate lower crowding and her overjet concern.
With moderate lower crowding and a 5 mm overjet she’s worried about, extractions are likely. Taking out #14 and #24 reduces the overjet and removes the #14 scissors bite. In the lower arch, #44/45 on the right and #34/35 on the left are all reasonable.
5.2
Links the lower extraction choice to the second molars: closing extraction space by moving the first molars forward frees room to upright the second molars.
Extraction of #35 #45 allow mesialization of #36 #46 which will give more space to align the impacted second molars. Some may choose to extract #44 instead, to align #43.
5.3
Plans to keep and upright both second molars and explains why extracting a second molar is not the preferred option here.
Both second molars have a good prognosis and are worth keeping. Extracting one and hoping the wisdom tooth replaces it is less predictable, because at age 13 you can't yet tell how the wisdom tooth will turn out.
5.4
Makes and justifies a decision about the lower third molars: keep them if extraction space allows uprighting without much distalisation; remove them if the second molars must move back and the third molars are in the way.
If the extraction space lets you upright mostly by moving the roots forward, the wisdom teeth may not need to come out. If you need to push the crowns back, the wisdom teeth will block you and may need removing first.
5.5
Describes appropriate uprighting mechanics for a partly erupted molar and how the attachment choice affects them.
If sufficient bonding surface is available, bond a tube (more feasible on #47). Uprighting can be achieved using a stiff base archwire with a piggyback wire, open coil spring, or uprighting spring. TAD (miniscrews) may also be considered, depending on retromolar space, mucosal conditions, and third molar position.
 
Bonus points
Mentions TADs (miniscrews) as an uprighting option and weighs their pros and cons. Pro: skeletal anchorage, so only the second molar moves and other teeth avoid reciprocal effects. Cons: an added procedure, loosening, discomfort, soft tissue covering the TAD in the retromolar area, extra cost, and the developing third molars in the way, which may need removing and are then lost as a backup.
Notes a TPA is optional, since the overjet is only 5 mm. But it is useful to add on distal extension hook from the TPA to correct scissors bite on #27.
Discusses anchorage: the reaction on the first molars and premolars during uprighting.
Notes that uprighting extrudes the molars, which suits her increased overbite, and checks the interocclusal clearance.
Offers a second plan, for example a non-extraction approach with third molar removal and distalisation, and explains why it is not their Plan A.
Follow-up questions (the tutor may use these word for word)
Which teeth would you extract, and why?
How does your extraction choice in the lower quadrant help the second molars?
Would you keep or remove the lower wisdom teeth? What would decide it?
Why not just extract #37 and let #38 take its place?
How would you upright #37 and #47?
Instructions to the tutor (not shown to students)
Require one justified plan covering both arches. A second plan is a bonus.
The orthodontic experts favoured an extraction plan: upper first premolars plus lower premolar extractions, with #44 or #45 on the right and #34 or #35 on the left, using first molar mesialisation to help uprighting. Accept other premolar choices when the student justifies them.
A non-extraction plan with third molar removal and distalisation was suggested by the oral surgeon. Accept it only if the student explains how the moderate lower crowding and the overjet will be corrected; probe this, since the orthodontists did not favour it.
Do not accept extraction of either second molar as the preferred option without challenge. Ask the student to weigh third molar unpredictability at age 13 against keeping a sound second molar and the long term monitoring required.
Accept either keeping or removing the lower third molars when the reasoning ties to the mechanics (root mesialisation vs crown distalisation) and the space available.
Carry forward the Phase 2 findings without adding new ones. No 3D imaging is available for this case.
Expert basis: Experts 1 and 2: extraction plan and first molar mesialisation to create uprighting space; keep both second molars. Expert 2: specific pattern U4s / #44 / #35, #14 extraction relieves the scissors bite, TPA optional, tube preferred, piggyback with open coil or lever arm, retromolar TADs difficult. Expert 1: reduce distalisation and favour root mesialisation where third molars are close; remove third molars if distalisation is needed and there is no room. Expert 3 (weighted, removal decisions): keep the second molars and remove the third molars rather than the second molars, as third molar morphology is unpredictable at 13; his non-extraction view on the overall plan carries less weight.
Questions you'd like to see
None for now.
Phase 6: Review the plan
What the student sees
Goal: Picture where treatment should end up, work back from that end point, and name the challenges you expect and what would make you change course.
Opening question: Picture the end of treatment under your plan. What challenges do you anticipate getting there?
What the tutor looks for, and what it reveals if a student is stuck
No.
What the tutor looks for
What the tutor reveals
6.1
Describes the end point and works backwards from it: where each molar, premolar and canine ends up, and the movements needed to get there.
At the end, both second molars should be upright in occlusion behind first molars that have moved forward, the overjet reduced, and #43 aligned.
6.2
States a reassessment checkpoint for each second molar and what triggers the fallback.
To check whether each second molar is actually uprighting after a few months. If not, may need to change mechanics of uprighting or explore other treatment plans.
6.3
Acknowledges the main risks: root resorption and mobility, a distal pocket or bony defect needing periodontal care, an open contact with food trapping, and collision with the third molars.
The main risks are root shortening and mobility, a deep pocket or bone defect behind the second molar that may need a periodontist, a gap that traps food, and running into the wisdom teeth.
6.4
Considers vertical and occlusal effects of uprighting the impacted second molars: extrusion of second molars, reciprocal intrusion/extrusion or tipping of anchorage teeth, and unwanted movement if the cantilever is activated outside the intended plane.
Uprighting impacted second molars may cause extrusion, leading to premature contacts, occlusal interference, and increased posterior vertical dimension. Reciprocal forces may induce intrusion, extrusion, or tipping of anchorage teeth, altering the occlusal plane. Improper cantilever activation may also result in unintended tooth movements.
 
Bonus points
Plans long-term monitoring of the remaining third molars after treatment.
Considers retention for the corrected scissors bites and crossbite.
Mentions treatment duration and cost as factors in her choice.
Follow-up questions (the tutor may use these word for word)
Where will each lower molar end up at the end of treatment?
Working back from that end point, is there anything you'd change?
What would you do if the molar isn't responding?
How would you explain the risks of uprighting to her?
Instructions to the tutor (not shown to students)
Defend an anticipated outcome rather than promising a guaranteed result. Link it to the chosen plan, the evidence and the patient's concerns.
Visualising the end point and working backwards to the mechanics is the skill the experts found hardest to teach. Prompt the student to describe final tooth positions before mechanics.
Make the uprighting checkpoint and fallback explicit for each second molar.
Carry forward the Phase 2 findings without adding new ones. No 3D imaging is available for this case.
Expert basis: Expert 2: work backwards from the end point (hardest skill to teach); distal pocket or bony defect and referral to perio; open contact; shared decision-making based on the patient's risk appetite. Expert 1: occlusal trauma from opposing occlusion; interocclusal clearance for molar extrusion; resorption and mobility with conical roots; visualising mechanics. Expert 3: cost and duration (bonus only).
Questions you'd like to see
None for now.
Closing question (asked once, after Phase 6): Looking back over the whole case, which factor had the biggest impact on how you managed the impacted second molars, and why?
 
Part 2: Messages used in every case
These are fixed and appear in all cases, not just Case 1. Text in [square brackets] is filled in automatically.
 
When a student is stuck
Backup question, if the tutor can't write its own plan for the student to critique: Which finding would you check first, and why?
Backup reveal, if the tutor can't write its own: [the reveal text from the phase] How would you use this in your plan?
When a phase ends with help, if the tutor's own acknowledgement can't be used: Let's move on to the next part.
Backup question, if the tutor is about to repeat itself and has no follow-up questions left: For this attempt ([number]), which part of the current goal remains unclear, and what evidence would help you address it?
 Our suggestion: "Which part of this are you still unsure about?"
 
When a student is confidently wrong
First, the tutor asks: What evidence or case finding supports that statement?
If the student is wrong again, the tutor starts its next question with: That statement is incorrect.
 
Closing messages
Default closing question, for any case without its own: Looking back, which finding or uncertainty had the greatest influence on your decision?
Final message: You have completed all [number] phases. Your learning summary is ready.
 
Backup questions if the AI is unavailable
After a wrong answer: Which finding in this case most directly conflicts with your current conclusion?
After a vague answer: Which specific case finding would make your answer clinically meaningful?
After a correct answer: What assumption in that reasoning would be most important to verify?
 
The More help button
Button: More help
Hover text: Ask the tutor for one more nudge. Your answer draft will stay in place.
Shown in the student's chat when pressed: More help requested
When it can't be used yet: More help becomes available after you submit an answer in this phase. It is unavailable after the tutor's full support step.
If it fails: The tutor could not prepare more help right now.
 
The learning summary
Headline, by score:
80 and above: Your reasoning is well backed by evidence
55 to 79: A sound start, with some gaps to go back over
Below 55: Try linking each decision to a finding in the case
Summary paragraph:
All phases finished: You finished all the phases and the reflection. The score reflects how well you explained your reasoning, not just your final answer.
Session ended early: You ended the session before finishing all the phases. This summary covers the reasoning you showed so far. Treat it as feedback to learn from.
Added when phases were finished with help: Phases [numbers] were completed with tutor support, not demonstrated independent mastery.
 Our suggestion: "Phases [numbers] were completed with help from the tutor."
Default strength: Kept working through the questions
Next steps:
Say what you see before you name a conclusion
Explain what each new test or image would tell you
Name one assumption that could change your plan
 
Phase labels in the summary: Not completed / Completed with tutor support / Completed independently / Completed — support not recorded
Our suggestion for the last one: "Completed (support not recorded)"
 
When no strength was recorded: The tutor did not single out a specific strength this time. That is a comment on one short session, not on you — work through the next steps and they are what the next summary will draw on.
Our suggestion: "The tutor did not single out a specific strength this time. That's about one short session, not about you. Work through the next steps, and the next summary will draw on them."
 
When no gaps were recorded: No specific gaps were recorded in this session. Keep making each step of your reasoning explicit so the tutor has something to test.
 
When no next steps were generated: No next steps were generated for this session. Revisit the case or ask your professor which part of the reasoning to practice first.
 
Part 3: How the tutor writes its own questions
The tutor follows these rules every time it writes a question. They're written here in plain English. Edit any rule, or add your own, and we'll update the tutor's instructions to match.
 
Use plain words and short sentences, the everyday clinical language a dental student would use at the chairside.
Each question asks exactly one thing.
A question is at most 45 words.
Before each question, write one short sentence (at most 20 words) about something specific the student said. Never use generic praise, never tell the student they've got it, and never agree with a wrong claim.
Never ask, or reword, a question already asked in the session, in any phase.
Never copy the phase goal or the points it's looking for into a question.
Don't give away the diagnosis or the management, and don't lecture.
Change approach as the student tries again: first probe their reasoning, then narrow the question or contrast two things, and from the third try, come at it from a different angle.
When a student is stuck after 2 answers without progress or presses More help: first offer a short plan for them to critique (at most 40 words), then, if still stuck, reveal the missing point in plain words (at most 50 words) and ask how they'd use it.
After 5 answers in a phase, reveal what's missing and move on, so no student gets stuck.
When a student says something confidently wrong, ask once for their basis, then say plainly that the statement is incorrect, without giving the answer.
Never suggest or ask about investigations that are not available in the case. If a student requests one, say it isn't available and redirect to the records provided.
Never give the answer because the student asks for it directly. Prompt, summarise or redirect instead, and wait for the student.
Ask the student to describe the end position of the teeth before discussing mechanics.
